text: Good evening. I call to order this November 5th, 2026, fiscal year 2028 to fiscal year 2033 capital budget public hearing and work session. We'll start this evening with disclosures. I'll go first. Thank you. With that, we'll move on to item number three, our public hearing. These are our procedures for public comment. Thank you for engaging with the school board through the public comment process. The school board welcomes comments from Loudoun County residents and believes that strong community engagement and outreach are important components of a successful school system. Speakers must limit comments to the time allotted. Based on the number of speakers and the agenda this evening, all speakers have been

allotted two minutes each for public comment. Please be advised that speakers who miss their time slot will not be called at a later time. Decorum and civility. All audience members shall maintain civility, decorum, and respect of the functioning and dignity of the school board at all times. Please remain seated unless arriving, departing, speaking at the podium, or during a break. Violations of civility, decorum, and respect include shouting, heckling, jeering, applause, and other noise which disrupts or delays the meeting,

obstructing speakers from being able to see the school board and vice versa, interrupting speakers, attempting to speak when not called to do so by the chair, and approaching a speaker or otherwise attempting to intimidate, disparage, or distract a speaker, staff member, or other meeting attendees. Speakers must refrain from vulgarity, obscenities, defamation, profanity, and other like breaches of disrespect, nor may speakers target, criticize, or attack individual students and/or individual division employees during public comment.

The school board requests that comments on an individual student or employee-related matter not be shared at public meetings where the disclosure could violate applicable confidentiality requirements. Speakers should communicate those concerns to their school principal or other appropriate school official. Speakers should face the dais and direct their comments to the school board per school board policy 2520. Members of the school board will not answer questions or

respond directly to the public during the public comment period. To the extent necessary, I will also warn of breaches of decorum, civility, and respect from attendees prior to taking other actions to preserve the orderly conduct of the meeting. Violations of decorum or civility by any meeting attendee may result in the chair directing staff to remove the attendee from the remainder of the meeting. Repeated or persistent violations of decorum or civility by the audience may result in, on the decision of the chair, public comment being tabled

until a later point in the meeting's agenda, limiting the number of attendees in the meeting room during public comment for safety reasons, or the public comment period ending for the evening. Distribution of materials to school board members. Copies of materials for board members should be given to the public information officer in the media box at the back of the boardroom before the start of the meeting. Please provide 12 copies of the materials. Under no circumstances may a speaker approach the dais. The public is reminded that access to school board meetings is available through

LCPS-TV on 1070 HD and Verizon Fios channel 43. The live stream of the meeting may be viewed on the website. We look forward to hearing your comments. We will now start with our virtual speakers. Our first virtual speaker is Caroline Price, followed by Ryan Schlesky. Great. Thank you. Can you hear me? Yes. Thank you. Good evening, school board members.

First, I want to thank you for your transparency with the last meeting, honesty, and willingness to speak up for our smaller schools. We appreciate your reassurance that closing these schools would not be considered and only as an absolute last resort. However, the enrollment numbers that were shared at the previous meeting were very eye-opening. We know that declining enrollment is coming, and I worry what that means for small schools like Lincoln Elementary. I'm asking the board to go beyond promising not to close these schools.

I'm asking to take proactive steps to protect them. One opportunity is revisiting previous attendance boundaries. Years ago, families living close to Lincoln were rezoned to Culbert and Banagher. While they're both wonderful schools, they're a little further away for families in Lincoln. Another opportunity is special permission. I understand the broader decision was delayed for special permission remains available, but with tighter restrictions. I ask the board to consider loosening some of the parameters.

This is personal for my family, as my daughter currently attends Lincoln, and my son hopes to join her in kindergarten next year. At a time when we're concerned about declining enrollment, why make it harder for families who want to attend these schools? You've spoken up about how much these schools mean for our communities, and my fear is in three or five years, Lincoln's enrollment will be too small that preserving it becomes harder. I'm asking for a plan, not just a promise. Please consider targeted boundary adjustments or more flexible distance-based

special permissions for under-enrolled schools while protecting the current students and incoming siblings. Thank you for your time. Thank you. Our actual final virtual speaker for this evening is Ryan Schlesky. Good evening, Chair and members of the board. I'm a Lucketts resident and parent. I ask the board to formally take consolidation and closure of all six of our small community rural schools off the table.

I appreciate the clarification that closures are not being recommended or considered, but identifying specific schools and potentially receiving schools made consolidation feel more like a developed plan than an idea. Please turn that reassurance into an official school board commitment. Lucketts Elementary is a center of gravity for our rural communities. All six of these schools anchor their communities, and we stand together. Lucketts shows why capital and operating decisions must align.

Records show that enrollment exceeded capacity in 2016. Accordingly, three additional classrooms were added in 2019. Today's utilization percentages must account for those earlier capacity decisions. The budget includes $10 million next year for high school practice turf fields and tennis court lighting. Meanwhile, it acknowledges deficiencies in Aldie and Lincoln, but neither are prioritized for the renovation program, partly

because of limited enrollment. Before approving those enhancements, please explain how documented needs to our small community rural schools will receive funding solutions. Please maintain and modernize all six of our small rural schools, align capital investments and enrollment projections, boundaries, and operating costs. Recognizing rural geography, transportation burdens, and the importance of keeping families connected to their schools.

A school's value cannot be reduced by a capacity percentage. Please formally take consolidation and closure off the table and adopt a capital plan that gives all six schools a sustainable future. Thank you for your time. Thank you. We'll now move on with our in-person speakers. Our first speaker is Christy Porter, followed by Matt

Rakowitz. I hope I got that right. And so our next speaker is Christy Porter. Evening, school board members. I wanted to start by saying thank you for continuing to support our small schools. We do appreciate it. And I have two boys, and one attended Lincoln Elementary and is now at Loudoun Valley High School, and the other is in third grade at Lincoln Elementary. I'm here tonight, like many others, to ask that the board take a proactive and

long-term approach to ensuring our small western schools don't just survive, but actually thrive. Lincoln Elementary is an exceptional school. I'm a little biased. However, I do have some data. For two consecutive years, it has earned the highest overall elementary school performance score in Loudoun County. It has received Virginia's Highest Achievement Award and Distinguished Designation, and in addition to these achievements, our student performance support framework

score for the last year was a 104.3, and in 2025, a 97.3. And both were the highest of all elementary schools for those years. We have outstanding tenured teachers, extraordinary community support, and generations of family in the community who have gone through these schools and who are totally invested. Why wouldn't we want more of this for more students? Clearly, this is an education experience that's working.

Past boundary decisions contributed to declining enrollment at our rural schools, and it's time to revisit those boundaries with an approach that respects established families. If we could grandfather families and their younger siblings into existing school pathways while phasing in new boundaries for families entering LCPS, I believe restoring our zoning would be met with less resistance, and I'm referring back to a debate that happened over the middle school rezoning. Expecting families already established in the Harmony and Woodgrove pathways to embrace reassignment was not overly realistic.

A phase-in of new families is a more realistic approach for the community. We would also continue to support special permission opportunities for small schools, especially for families who drive right past Lincoln to reach their assigned schools. And this isn't only a Lincoln issue, this is happening across the area. Thoughtful enrollment planning could strengthen Lincoln, Hamilton, and other rural- Thank you. Our next speaker is Matt Rakowitz, followed by James Simmons.

Good evening. This evening, I'm speaking as a parent from one of Loudoun's smallest elementary schools and its largest middle school. Dr. Rashid, thank you for visiting Aldie yesterday. You looked great online in Aldie blue. More importantly, your presence spoke volumes. You demonstrated meaningful community engagement, and I'm grateful to have you representing the Little River District. Thank you to Carrie Labell for welcoming us to your roundtable this week, to John Pepper and to April Chandler for your kind emails in support of small schools.

Those things go very well noticed. We appreciate Aldie's approved walking track and inclusive playgrounds, along with the proposed capital improvements over the next several years. And as we approach our 100th anniversary, I urge the school board to follow through on these investments in the school that has served generations of Loudoun families and to include parents early in future rezoning discussions. At Willard, which is the county's largest middle school and the only middle school

with modular buildings, enrollment exceeds capacity, with students attending classes in those separate buildings, yet smaller high schools receive three school security officers, and Willard only receives two. I asked John Clark and Dr. Spence to evaluate adding a third officer at Willard based on enrollment and campus layout and not just on the label middle school. Finally, to look for these funding opportunities, I echo Amy Ricardi's sentiment

last week when enrollment was compared with 2016 levels. Yet non-school-facing staffing has increased by roughly 100 FTEs since that same level of enrollment in 2016, and I didn't hear any discussion about those. And so I did some FOIA requests, and I would encourage the board to transparently conduct an evaluation of the non-school-facing FTEs before considering any further reductions to teachers, staff, or student-facing resources.

Thank you so much for all the work that you do. It's very much appreciated. Thank you. Our final speaker this evening is James Simmons. Good evening. My name is Jim Simmons. I'm a Loudoun County resident, and my home is zoned for Lincoln Elementary. My wife and I bought our house largely because of that school, and we have two young children who we expect to send there shortly.

I'm here tonight because I'm deeply concerned about the proposal to close schools in Western Loudoun. I want to say plainly that the way it was presented to the public was irresponsible. Families found out that their neighborhood schools could be shut down through a presentation with little context, little notice, and no opportunity for the people affected to weigh in first. It caused real fear in families across Western Loudoun and showed a total lack of respect for the parents and the communities who rely on these schools and who trusted this board and this administration to work with them.

Schools like Lincoln anchor neighborhoods. They're why families move here, invest here, and stay here despite struggling with the very high cost that this county presents. A decision to close a school changes the community permanently, and such an option should never be presented as flippantly as it was the other night. If cuts are truly necessary, and it sounds like they are, then I would echo Ms. Ricardi's comments from last week and ask that this board first look within the

walls of this building. I would then ask that this board look at the pet projects, programs, and spending that do not directly serve the education of Loudoun students. Our children's classrooms should be the last place that your budget cuts reach, not the first. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you all for providing us with your public comment this evening. We appreciate the opportunity to hear from you.

And with that, we will move on to the next item on our agenda, which is item number 4.01, our work session, provided by the Department of Support Services, the superintendent's recommended fiscal year 2028 to 2033 capital budget. Presented this evening by Adnan Mamu and Mr. Trainer.

Good evening, Chair Chandler, Vice Chair Donahue, members of the board, and Dr. Spence. We are back here today to continue our conversation about the superintendent's recommended capital budget. On October 27th, we presented the summary of the changes that are in the superintendent's recommendation for the capital budget.

And then tonight, we will be going into the details of those programs and the different projects that make up that capital budget. And then the next capital budget work session is scheduled for November 30th. And then the school board adoption is scheduled for December 15th. So, this is also available on page 13 of the capital budget

book, so we're not expecting anybody to try and read the small print here. What I would like to point out is that the overall budget is not changing for FY28 and FY29. So the $83.5 million for our capital budget remains the same, as well as our capital asset preservation program cap budget for 65.1 million, and we'll go into the details of

what those line items are later in our presentation. So here's a quick summary of the capital budget of 83.5 million by category. As you can see, the largest portion of it goes towards our student program space, including visual and performing arts, CTAE space, Roby, outdoor learning, independent living labs, and the elementary school classroom

additions, which we're going to go into a little bit more detail in a few slides. And then the next largest is infrastructure improvement, which includes life cycle replacement of furniture, unified communication, security improvements, and kitchen equipment. 15% of the budget's for bus and white fleet, and the rest are athletics, safety and security enhancements, playgrounds, privacy restrooms, and support spaces.

So here's, again, a presentation of the summary of the changes. The changes are highlighted in blue here. The superintendent's recommendation includes building elementary classroom additions at Guilford, Sterling, and Leesburg Elementary, as well as $9.3 million in safety and security initiatives. This is not going to change the overall budget, and we're going to go into where

the funding we're recommending to come from for these enhancements So for the elementary classroom additions, the superintendent's recommendation is to expedite building additions at Guilford, Sterling, and Leesburg Elementary School. And we are proposing to be able to do these additions by deferring classroom additions that were previously identified in

the FY28 and 29 budget for Eagle Ridge Middle School, as well as Farmwell Station Middle School. These elementary additions, we're calling them classroom additions. However, these are mainly to address some space needs at these buildings because at the time of their construction, there was a lot of spaces that were not included in that building design, including small group breakout spaces as well as individual instruction spaces.

So the design and construction for these additions would include the necessary spaces that these schools need. The enhancement also includes initiatives for district-wide improvements for $9.3 million, and which is going to come out of the deferment for the middle school additions. So I wanted to quickly go over the timeline so that

everybody's expectations can align when these projects are going to be designed and constructed, and when we can expect to see these additions completed. So typically, once a project is funded, there's a nine-to-12-month period of we have to go through zoning approval prior to us being able to move forward with the project. And during that process, we also start the design of that building, which typically

takes nine to 12 months, and then 12 to 18 months of construction. So the estimated timeline is, after funding begins, roughly two and a half to three years. So for Guilford, Sterling, and Leesburg, if the funding is available in FY28, the completion is estimated to be FY31, which is school year 2030. Now I'm going to pass it on to Mr. Treanor to take us through the rest of the presentation.

Okay. Good evening. And so, to directly answer one of Mr. Svenson's questions previously, you had asked about the two middle schools and what was happening if we deferred those renovation project or the addition projects of both. So we've broken out here, these two pages come from the school pages that are listed in the back of the book, 150 and 188.

And they go through a great deal of detail listing the different projects that are coming up for both Eagle Ridge and Farmwell Station. Particularly, I want to call your attention to the critical system replacement coming up at Farmwell Station in 2029. That is a complete system replacement of the mechanical system in that building. And then we've got the restroom privacy projects that are currently listed in '31 and '32, although we hope that we can accelerate those if we can get additional

funding from the county on the year-end process this year. And there'll be more on that coming up at a future slide. And then next slide, we're going down the list of career and technical education. The CTAE program, as it's called, it's a multi-year program, runs across the entire physical budget for the capital improvement program.

And as part of that project, our team is working very closely with Dr. Grubbs and the CTAE office, as well as teaching and learning, or, well, it is teaching and learning, but as well as school leadership to identify what CTAE labs and classrooms are really the priority for them as they come up with renovations. And so in the FY27 program, as this slide identifies, we're doing the

family and consumer science project renovation, classroom renovations, labs in our four oldest middle schools. We're also going to be doing a FACS and then adding a culinary kitchen at Loudoun County High School. And those are all in process. As part of construction in '27, we have also added the HAMS site spaces at Briarwood and Tuscarora. And then for the '28 program, which is what you're going to be approving this

year's budget, we are going to design or we're going to do the construction of the FACS classrooms at those four middle schools. Plus, we're going to be designing the FACS classroom renovations for Farmwell Station, for Eagle Ridge, and Harper Park. And then tentatively in FY29, we plan the construction of Farmwell Station, Eagle Ridge, Harper Park FACS classrooms.

That's I say tentative because we're still working very closely to better define the FY29 program and make sure that we've got the funding to do all of those, along with the other CTAE initiatives that Dr. Grubbs and team are advocating for. Next up, we've got visual and performing arts. And of course, this has been a focus of the school board for the past several years, and we are actively working with our architects and engineers to design the first four projects right now.

And our recommended FY28 capital budget includes the start of construction for Broad Run, Loudoun Valley, and Stone Bridge. And then as we have briefed last year, the work at Loudoun County High School is being deferred until FY29 to go into a larger campus-wide master plan renovation and some changes there that we're planning.

Next up, we've got independent living labs. Last summer, we completed the construction at Dominion, Rock Ridge, Stone Bridge High School, and Woodgrove High School. For this upcoming summer in the FY28 budget, we're planning to do the living labs at Broad Run, John Champ, Potomac Falls, and Tuscarora. All of the high schools will be done as we move forward and then in the future

years, and then we will transition to putting these classrooms also in our middle schools. And next up is our high school athletics, which is actually two separate projects in the capital budget, the high school practice fields, which includes an artificial turf field and lights. So we have approximately half of our high schools were only built with one artificial turf field in the stadium.

The other half have two artificial turf fields. They have one in the stadium, and they have a practice field adjacent to it. Unfortunately, the practice field at the time it was built at the schools that have it does not have lighting. And so this project adds a second artificial turf field to the schools that only have one, and it adds lights to that field. Then the schools that have two artificial turf fields, it adds lights to those

fields. And, of course, if you've had any conversations with our athletic program, they are stretched really hard trying to fit all of the different sports teams into the practices on these fields during daylight hours, especially now as it's getting dark at 5:00. And so they're anxiously awaiting this work. The chart you see there, and then the second project is tennis court lighting, and so that's adding lighting to all of our tennis courts at all of our high schools.

The chart on the right-hand side will be referred to as tennis. That means it's getting tennis court lights that year. Where it's turf, it's getting the turf field added, and lights means it is getting the lights for that turf field. And so as you can see, and I highlight Woodgrove is getting the tennis court lights we're funding in FY27. Or sorry, let me back up. Woodgrove is getting the athletic field lights in 2027,

but it's not getting the tennis court lights that year. We have delayed Woodgrove because we're working with trying to develop a master plan for that campus. There's some initiative looking to potentially add onto the building for a CTAE program, and the addition would likely be in the location of the tennis courts. So we don't want to put the lights on just yet till we've got that plan finalized. But this is a multi-year program, as you can see.

We also had to adjust the order of the schools from what we presented to you last year, because we're working through a challenge with county coding or the county ordinance where the athletic field lighting color is restricted by ordinance, so we're having to go through the process and get an approval for the brighter color lights than what is currently allowed in the ordinance within

the county. The towns within the county, their ordinance allows the higher color light, higher temperature lights for the athletic fields. And so we've moved Heritage and Tuscarora further up because we can proceed with those right now under the town's zoning, as we work through the process on the others to try to get the zoning amendment approved there. And so, we're starting that process now for all of these schools

and don't expect it to impact the total length of the project, but we did need to flip some schools in order to keep the project moving smoothly while we're going through that process with the county. And then this slide, similar to one that Mr. Mimms showed you earlier, estimated timelines. We're doing this again just to explain here, we've got a zoning process, we've got a design process, and a construction process.

So these, the lights that you funded in the FY27 program, we are expecting completion of those, the lights, the fields, in 2029 physical year. And so it's approximately a two-year process and there is obviously great expectations that when they see a project listed, that it's going to be completed immediately. And we are working very hard to try to get those done as fast as possible, but it's

a very regimented process that we go through, working with the county and our architects and then our contractors to get these built. Next up are our school buses. Our school bus replacement program is another line in our capital budget. And in line with our fleet modernization plan, we are purchasing 61 buses in FY28 as part of the superintendent's recommended budget.

You'll see the breakout there for FY28, where we're getting a mixture of three gas buses, but then the majority of our buses purchased next year are propane. And then you see, of course, our 10-year goal on the master plan is to ultimately get to 85% of our bus fleet as propane, 10% diesel, and then the 5% would be a mix between the electric gas buses and basically, which are the only two

options we have left. But, and then the second project listed on this is the bus washing station. That is an existing facility adjacent to our central fueling station that was built to be a bus washing station. But a little over 20 years ago, that building was repurposed to be a small engine repair shop for the facilities grounds team, and we're still in it. It was a temporary move at the time, and unfortunately, it's been much longer than

any of us planned. But, we already have an approved project that will do the joint storage facility for the salt storage, the pole barns for the equipment, and then the small engine shop that's going to be built on the opposite end of the transportation building. And once that project, it's going through the approval process now. We've got zoning approval. We're going through, working with the county, finalizing and working the design of

that. That project will start under construction, we hope, in the next and approximately a year. And then once the small engine shop is able to move out of the wash bay, we'll be able to go back into the wash bay as part of this project and reinstall the bus washing equipment and give us the ability to wash the buses, automated system, which will help us in preserving the life cycle of our existing bus fleet.

And then another big project, our playground project. This one was clearly a priority for the board several years ago. We listened very closely to that. We've listed out the different schools, as everybody likes to see the schools, the way the projects have already been done and what's coming up. You'll see in FY28, we have 11 of the new full inclusive playgrounds planned, and the schools are listed there. Then we transition, and in FY29 to 32, we're going to

start going through and building the two to five-year-old playgrounds where they will fit on the campus. We're going to have some schools where it's going to be a huge challenge to fit that in. But that is the follow on. And so this will keep moving at about the same pace with a large number of schools each year. And very well-received program, as I know you guys are getting feedback too from our families.

And then we have several smaller projects on this slide, four separate projects that are recurring funding lines in our capital budget for school furniture, the school kitchen equipment on the cafeteria school nutrition side, security equipment, lifecycle replacements, and then the unified communication system, which is a newer system we're putting in that wraps the intercom system, the clocks and the bells all into one system in our schools.

And so, you'll see on the UCS system excuse me, that project's managed by the Department of Digital Innovation, and they're approximately three-quarters of the way finished getting that rolled out to every school. And so they're making very good progress on that one. Next up, our outdoor learning spaces. In FY27, you approved funding for this to get this process started. Our Office of Sustainability is working very closely with

our construction design team, school leadership, and teaching and learning. And this year they're identifying pilot locations for these classrooms. And then our FY28 program incorporates funding to try to construct these pilot classrooms, outdoor learning classrooms. Next up, restroom privacy and safety improvements. So this project was previously funded in FY27 and

partially funded in FY27. Stone Bridge High School would use prior year funding to be able to work that this summer. Based on feedback that we received from the school board in our work sessions in June, we have worked to try to identify a way to accelerate these projects. And so you'll be seeing a request next week for additional funding through the county's end of year funding process.

If approved, the current plan that we have is Stone Bridge starting next summer with our FY27 funding, and then Briarwood, Stream, and Tuscarora would be the following year using the FY28 funding. We have an expedited plan that if we are successful in getting the 14.6 million in the county end of year process, we would accelerate that and do eight high schools

later this year into the summer timeframe, and then have funding to do 10 high schools in FY28. That then would allow us to accelerate, to expedite per se, the middle schools, and we're proposing to do six middle schools a year, '29, '30, and '31. And that would then complete all of our schools. We're just caution, we looked at trying to how we could expedite the middle

schools, and at the moment, we're not comfortable trying to do that. We think that the middle schools present a little different challenge. Most of them are not two story, and we're concerned about the way they're set up with the house set up and how we're going to get these restrooms to fit. We haven't designed that out yet. But as I said, we've got a plan. We're excited to do this. And as a reminder, the three schools that have it, Dominion, Heritage, and

Woodgrove, very well received. The students love it. The staff loves it. We got very positive feedback from the families that have seen them. And so this project would allow us to move forward with that. And we're ready to go. You'll see that funding request next week. And then support space. We'll touch on this briefly.

And I'll share that we have tentatively identified a location for the FACE Hub, but we're going through our internal review process now to ensure that the site will meet all of our LCPS requirements. And so we're not ready to publicly disclose the location yet, but we're getting close. And next week you'll also see a funding request for some year-end funds to facilitate accelerating the build-out of that space to do it this year.

So ideally, we would be able to open the FACE Hub next summer of '27. And get it operational.
